newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gore praises S.African wildlife partnerships.
newsitem.headline: Gore praises S.African wildlife partnerships.

text.p: U.S. Vice-President Al Gore toured a wildlife reserve near the Indian Ocean port of Durban on Saturday and said more cities around the world should seek to preserve their natural environment.

Gore accompanied by wife Tipper and two of his children, Albert and Sarah, visited the Shongweni reserve. Gore is on a three-day visit to South Africa for talks that will focus on trade, scientific and environmental issues.
"This Shongweni reserve is an example of what conservationists and municipal authorities can do together in partnership," Gore said.
"It's a magnificent example of an urban wildlife reserve -- the only one of it's kind I have seen. I think it ought to be emulated elsewhere."
Gore was hosted by naturalist Ian Player, elder brother of golfer Gary Player, who hailed the Vice-President as a world leader on conservation.
"I pray to God he will be guided to continue to lead the world into the next century," Player said.

Gore arrived in South Africa on Friday. After meeting labour union leaders in Durban later on Saturday, he travels to Cape Town where he will head the U.S. side to the U.S.-South Africa binational commission which meets about every six months.
The South African side is headed by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki. The two leaders are likely to focus on foreign affairs in private one-on-one discussions in Cape Town.

The United States and South Africa exchanged angry words last month when Washington warned Pretoria against going through with a proposed $650 million sale of a laser-guided tank firing control system to Syria.
South African President Nelson Mandela angrily rejected the U.S. criticism as an affront to his country's national pride and independence.
Washington warned providing the system to Syria, which it classifies as a "state sponsor of terrorism", would result in South Africa losing $120 million of U.S. aid.

Gore, who seems certain to run for president in the year 2000, has emerged as a key player in U.S. foreign policy. Last week he chaired important talks with Russia and next month will head a delegation to China.
In Cape Town Gore will pay courtesy calls on Mandela and retired archbishop Desmond Tutu. He will also tour the former island prison where Mandela was held for 18 years.
